unit.title: Perform manual soldering/de-soldering of electrical/electronic components

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Where should a hot soldering iron be put down when you are not using it?
options: Flat on the bench, with the tip pointing away from you
On top of the circuit board you are working on
Hanging by its cable over the edge of the bench
In its proper stand, away from the cable and the edge

questions.stem: Why must you not eat or drink at the bench when using tin-lead solder?
options: Food crumbs make the solder joints go dull and grainy
Lead from the solder can pass from your hands to food
A spilled drink makes the soldering iron cool too fast
The flux fumes make any food at the bench go bad

questions.stem: Why should a fume extractor be used when soldering?
options: Flux fumes can harm your lungs and cause asthma
It cools the joint so that the solder sets faster
It keeps dust off the circuit board while you work
It stops the solder from sticking to the iron tip

questions.stem: You burn a finger on a soldering iron. What is the right first aid?
options: Put butter or oil on the burn straight away
Burst any blister so that the skin can dry
Hold it under cool running water for 20 minutes
Cover it tightly with sticky tape to keep the air out

questions.stem: Before you switch on a mains-powered soldering station, what should you check?
options: That the cable, plug and casing are not damaged
That the tip has been filed to a sharp point
That the sponge is so wet that water drips from it
That the bench is covered with paper to catch solder

questions.stem: Why do you wear an anti-static wrist strap when handling some electronic components?
options: To keep your wrist from getting tired while working
To stop you getting a shock from the mains supply
To hold the components in place on the board
To stop static electricity from damaging the parts

questions.stem: How should static-sensitive parts, such as integrated circuits (ICs), be stored until they are used?
options: Loose in a plastic tray with other parts
Wrapped in kitchen foil and a plastic bag
In anti-static bags or tubes
Pushed into a block of ordinary packing foam

questions.stem: What is "tinning" the tip of a soldering iron?
options: Filing the tip until the copper shows through
Coating the hot tip with fresh solder
Wrapping the tip in tin foil to keep it clean
Dipping the tip in water to cool it before use

questions.stem: How should you clean the tip of a hot soldering iron while you are working?
options: Scrape it with a file or with sandpaper
Wipe it on a damp sponge or brass wool
Dip it into a cup of cold water
Rub it on a cloth or your work clothes

questions.stem: Which soldering iron is best for small electronic joints on a circuit board?
options: A large 100 W iron made for roofing work
A gas blowtorch set to a small, hot flame
A soldering gun with a heavy copper loop
A temperature-controlled iron with a fine tip

questions.stem: For ordinary tin-lead solder, which tip temperature is often used for circuit board work? (Always follow the solder maker's data.)
options: About 300–350 °C
About 100–150 °C
About 180–200 °C
About 550–600 °C

questions.stem: What does the flux in cored solder do?
options: It makes the solder joint stronger once it has cooled
It colours the joint so that you can see it clearly
It cleans the metal so the solder can flow
It insulates the joint so that no current can leak

questions.stem: At about what temperature does 63/37 tin-lead solder melt?
options: About 100 °C
About 450 °C
About 1 000 °C
About 183 °C

questions.stem: How is lead-free solder different from tin-lead solder when you use it?
options: It melts at a lower temperature than tin-lead
It needs no flux at all to make a good joint
It melts at a higher temperature than tin-lead
It can only be used on wires, not on boards

questions.stem: Why must component leads and board pads be clean before soldering?
options: Dirt and oxide stop the solder from wetting the metal
Clean parts make the solder change colour when hot
Dirty parts make the iron tip wear out more slowly
Dirt on the leads makes the component's value change

questions.stem: On a diode, what does the painted band at one end show?
options: The anode (positive) end
The cathode end
The value in ohms
The maximum voltage

questions.stem: How can you tell which lead of a new LED is the anode (positive)?
options: It is the shorter lead
It is the lead on the flat side
It is the longer lead
It is the lead with a bend in it

questions.stem: On an aluminium electrolytic capacitor, what does the stripe down one side usually mark?
options: The negative lead
The positive lead
The capacitance value
The top of the part

questions.stem: A resistor has colour bands brown, black, red, then gold. What is its value?
options: 1 kΩ

questions.stem: On an integrated circuit (IC), how do you find pin 1?
options: It is always the pin nearest the printed name
It is next to the notch or dot on the body
It is the longest pin on the package
It is the pin in the middle of each side

questions.stem: When you bend a resistor's leads to fit the board holes, where should the bend be?
options: Right against the body, as tight as possible
A little way from the body, using pliers
Anywhere, by twisting the lead with your fingers
At the very tip of the lead, after soldering

questions.stem: What is the right way to solder a component lead to a pad on a circuit board?
options: Melt solder on the tip, then carry it to the joint
Put solder on the pad, then push the lead into it
Heat the pad and lead together, then feed in solder
Heat the solder wire only, and let it drip on the pad

questions.stem: When the joint is made, in which order do you take things away?
options: Take the iron away first, then the solder wire
Take both away at once, with a quick flick of the wrist
Leave the iron on the joint until the solder smokes
Take the solder wire away first, then the iron

questions.stem: Why must the joint not be moved while the solder is cooling?
options: Movement gives a weak, grainy (disturbed) joint
Movement makes the solder cool down too slowly
Movement makes the joint shine far too much
Movement pushes flux into the component body

questions.stem: How long should the iron usually stay on a small circuit board joint?
options: A few seconds, just long enough for the solder to flow
About one full minute, to be sure the pad is hot enough
Until the board starts to turn brown around the pad
Less than a tenth of a second, so nothing heats up

questions.stem: What does a good tin-lead solder joint on a board look like?
options: A dull, grey ball sitting on top of the pad
Smooth and shiny, sloping in onto the pad
A large blob that hides the lead and the pad
Rough and cracked where it meets the lead

questions.stem: A joint is dull, grainy and shaped like a ball. What is the most likely fault?
options: A solder bridge to the next pad
Too much flux left on the board
A lifted copper pad under the joint
A dry joint, not heated enough

questions.stem: What is a solder bridge?
options: A wire link fitted on purpose across the board
A crack across the middle of a solder joint
Solder that wrongly joins two pads or tracks
The bend in a component lead above the board

questions.stem: Why is a cold (dry) joint a problem, even if it looks connected?
options: It makes the board heavier than it should be
It makes the component work at a higher voltage
It may give a poor connection that fails later
It changes the colour code of the resistor

questions.stem: Why might you clip a heat sink, such as a crocodile clip, on a lead while soldering it?
options: To hold the board still on the bench
To earth the component to stop static
To make the solder flow faster into the hole
To draw heat away so the part is not damaged

questions.stem: Why do you slide heat-shrink sleeving onto a wire before soldering a joint?
options: So the wire does not get hot while soldering
Because it cannot be fitted once the joint is made
So the solder flows inside the sleeving
To hold the two wires together while soldering

questions.stem: Before soldering a stranded wire to a terminal, what should you do to the bare end?
options: Twist the strands and tin them
Cut off half the strands so that it fits easily
Spread the strands out flat, like an open fan
Fold the bare end back over the insulation

questions.stem: After you solder a wire to a terminal, the insulation has melted back. What caused this?
options: The solder wire had too much flux in its core
The wire was not tinned before it was soldered
The terminal was cleaned before soldering began
The iron was held on the joint for too long

questions.stem: What is a desoldering pump (solder sucker) used for?
options: To suck melted solder away from a joint
To blow flux fumes away from your face
To pump fresh solder into a joint
To cool a joint quickly after soldering

questions.stem: How is desoldering braid (wick) used?
options: Wrap it round the component lead and pull hard
Melt it into the joint to add extra copper strength
Lay it on the joint and heat it to soak up solder
Dip it in water and press it on the hot joint

questions.stem: What can happen if you heat a pad for too long while de-soldering?
options: The component will change its value for ever
The copper pad or track can lift off the board
The solder will turn into flux and run away
The board will become a better conductor

questions.stem: A component with several leads must be removed. What is the best way?
options: Pull it out hard while heating one lead at a time
Clear the solder from every lead, then lift it out
Cut the board around the part with a hacksaw
Heat the body of the part until it falls out

questions.stem: What helps you inspect small solder joints closely?
options: A bright torch held right up against the board
A pair of dark safety sunglasses
A magnifier, such as a loupe or lamp
A small mirror held behind the board

questions.stem: What is commonly used to clean flux residue off a board after soldering?
options: Isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush
Water and washing powder, then a hot oven
Petrol on a rag
Sandpaper rubbed over the joints

questions.stem: When you trim component leads after soldering, what should you do?
options: Cut them with scissors right down into the joint
Leave them full length so they can be tested later
Bend them flat across the board onto the next pad
Hold or cover the end so the clipping does not fly

questions.stem: Which item of PPE is most important when soldering and trimming leads?
options: A hard hat
Ear defenders
Safety glasses
Rubber boots

questions.stem: On a circuit board, what are the copper "tracks"?
options: Holes for fixing the board into its case
Labels that show the name of each part
Places where the board is allowed to bend
Copper paths that join the parts together

questions.stem: Which solder wire is best for small circuit board joints?
options: Thick plumbing solder, 3 mm or more across
Thin flux-cored solder, about 0.5–1 mm across
Solid solder with no flux, about 5 mm across
Acid-core solder made for sheet-metal work

questions.stem: After soldering a small kit, how should it first be checked?
options: Inspect each joint, then check it with a meter
Connect it straight to the mains to see if it works
Shake it hard to see whether any parts fall off
Put it straight into its case and screw it shut

questions.stem: How should used solder scraps, dross and lead clippings be disposed of?
options: Washed down the sink with plenty of water
Put in a marked container for safe disposal
Mixed in with food waste in the kitchen bin
Left in the iron's stand for the next class

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Name the cutting tool used to trim component leads close to the board after soldering.
What do the letters PCB stand for?
What do the letters ESD stand for?
A resistor is marked red, red, brown. What is its value in ohms?
Name the electric tool that blows hot air, used to shrink heat-shrink sleeving.
In 60/40 solder, which metal makes up the 60 per cent?
What is the name of the coating, often green, on a circuit board that stops solder sticking where it is not wanted?
What is the unit of capacitance?
In a resistor value such as 4.7 kΩ, the letter k stands for how many?
What name is given to components whose leads pass through holes in the board and are soldered on the other side?
What do the letters SMD stand for?
What is the name of the board with parallel copper strips and rows of holes, used to build test circuits?
Name the holder with clips on arms, used to hold a board or wires steady while you solder.
What is the unit of electrical resistance?
What is the name of the flat, wide tip shape, like a small screwdriver blade, used for larger joints?

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of manual soldering, and say how each one is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Burns: the tip of the iron is very hot, often over 300 °C, so I always put the iron back in its stand, never touch the tip or the metal near it, and let joints cool before handling them. Fumes: heated flux gives off fumes that can harm the lungs and cause asthma, so I use a fume extractor or work in a well-ventilated area and keep my face out of the smoke. Lead: tin-lead solder contains lead, so I do not eat, drink or smoke at the bench, and I wash my hands after work. Flying clippings: when trimming leads I wear safety glasses and hold or cover the lead end. Shock and fire: I check the iron's cable, plug and casing before use, keep the cable away from the hot tip, keep paper off the bench, and switch the iron off when I finish.
markingPoints: Burns: use the stand, do not touch the tip, let joints cool
Fumes: fume extractor or good ventilation
Lead: no eating or drinking at the bench; wash hands
Flying clippings: safety glasses, hold or cover lead ends
Shock and fire: check cable and plug, keep cable from tip, clear bench, switch off

essays.stem: Explain what static electricity can do to electronic components, and describe how you would protect them at the workbench.
essays.modelAnswer: Static electricity builds up on our bodies and clothes as we move, especially on plastic chairs or floors. When we touch a component, the charge can jump into it. We may not feel it, but it can damage or weaken parts such as integrated circuits and transistors, so they fail at once or some time later. To protect them, I work on an anti-static mat connected to the earth point, and I wear an anti-static wrist strap clipped to the same point. I keep sensitive parts in their anti-static bags or tubes until I need them. I handle boards and parts by their edges and do not touch the pins. I keep plastic bags, foam cups and other things that build up static away from the bench, and I use an earthed soldering station where possible.
markingPoints: Static builds up on the body and clothes and can jump to parts
It can damage parts at once or weaken them so they fail later
Uses an anti-static mat and wrist strap connected to the earth point
Keeps parts in anti-static bags or tubes until use
Handles parts by the edges and keeps static-making materials away

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare the soldering iron and your work before soldering a set of components onto a circuit board.
essays.modelAnswer: I set up on a clear, tidy bench with good light and a fume extractor, and with an anti-static mat and wrist strap where they are needed. I check the iron's cable, plug and stand, wet the sponge so that it is damp but not dripping, and fit a tip of the right size for the joints. I switch on and set the temperature to suit the solder, as the maker advises. When the tip is hot, I wipe it on the sponge and tin it with a little fresh solder. I check the parts list and the board layout, and identify each component, its value and which way round it goes. I clean any dirty pads or leads, bend the leads to fit the holes, and fit the parts, starting with the lowest ones.
markingPoints: Sets up a clear bench with light, fume extraction and static protection
Checks the iron, cable, plug and stand; damp sponge; right tip
Sets the temperature and tins the tip
Identifies each part, its value and which way round it fits
Cleans and forms leads and fits the lowest parts first

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to solder a through-hole resistor onto a circuit board.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the resistor's value from its colour bands and check its place on the board layout. I bend the leads with pliers, a little away from the body, so they fit the holes, and push the resistor in flat against the board. I bend the leads out slightly on the solder side to hold it in place. I wipe the hot, tinned tip on the damp sponge. I place the tip so that it touches both the pad and the lead at the same time, and after about a second I feed solder into the joint, not onto the tip. When the solder has flowed around the lead and covered the pad, I take the solder away first and then the iron. I keep the board still while the joint cools. Then I trim the lead just above the joint with side cutters, holding the end, and inspect the joint.
markingPoints: Identifies the value and the place on the board
Forms the leads away from the body and fits the part flat
Heats the pad and lead together with a clean, tinned tip
Feeds solder into the joint, then removes solder before the iron
Does not move the joint while cooling; trims safely and inspects

essays.stem: Describe what a good solder joint looks like, and name three faults to look for, saying what causes each one.
essays.modelAnswer: A good joint on a circuit board is smooth and, with tin-lead solder, bright and shiny. The solder covers the whole pad and rises up the lead in a neat concave slope, like a small volcano, and the outline of the lead can still be seen. Lead-free joints look a little duller but should still be smooth. A cold or dry joint looks dull, grainy or lumpy and may sit like a ball; it is caused by not heating the pad and lead enough, or by dirt. A solder bridge is solder joining two pads or tracks that should be separate; it is caused by too much solder or by dragging the iron. A disturbed joint looks frosty and cracked; it is caused by moving the lead before the solder has set. A lifted pad is caused by too much heat for too long.
markingPoints: Good joint: smooth, shiny, pad covered, concave slope up the lead
Cold or dry joint and its cause
Solder bridge and its cause
Disturbed joint or lifted pad and its cause
Notes that lead-free joints look slightly duller

essays.stem: Explain why some components must be fitted the right way round. Give three examples and say how each one is marked.
essays.modelAnswer: Some components only work properly, or only stay safe, when current flows through them in one direction. If they are fitted the wrong way round, the circuit will not work, and some parts can be damaged or even burst. A diode has a painted band at one end, which marks the cathode; it must match the band shown on the board. An LED has a longer lead, which is the anode, and a flat edge on the rim of its body next to the cathode lead. An aluminium electrolytic capacitor has a stripe with minus signs down one side to mark the negative lead, and its positive lead is usually longer; if it is fitted the wrong way, it can overheat and burst. An integrated circuit has a notch or dot at one end to show pin 1, which must line up with the mark on the board.
markingPoints: Explains that polarised parts only work one way and can be damaged
Diode: band marks the cathode
LED: longer lead is the anode; flat edge by the cathode
Electrolytic capacitor: stripe marks the negative lead
IC: notch or dot marks pin 1

essays.stem: Compare using a desoldering pump and desoldering braid to remove a component. Describe how each one is used.
essays.modelAnswer: A desoldering pump, or solder sucker, is a spring-loaded tube. I push the plunger down to set it, heat the joint with the iron until the solder melts, then put the nozzle on the melted solder and press the button. The pump sucks the solder away. It is quick and good for clearing holes with a lot of solder, but the nozzle needs cleaning often and it may leave a thin film. Desoldering braid is a flat copper braid that contains flux. I lay a clean part of the braid on the joint and press the hot iron on top. The solder melts and soaks into the braid, which I lift away while it is still hot, and then I cut off the used end. Braid is very good for small amounts of solder and flat pads, but it uses up braid and heats the pad for longer.
markingPoints: Pump: set, heat, place nozzle, release
Pump: quick for holes with plenty of solder; needs cleaning
Braid: clean braid on joint, iron on top, lift while hot
Braid: cut off used end; good for small amounts and flat pads
Takes care not to overheat pads with either method

essays.stem: Describe how to join two stranded wires end to end by soldering, and how the joint should be insulated.
essays.modelAnswer: First I cut a piece of heat-shrink sleeving a little longer than the joint and slide it onto one wire, well away from where the heat will be. I strip a short length of insulation from each wire without cutting any strands. I twist the strands of each wire neatly and tin them with a little solder. I then join the two wires so that they hold together firmly before soldering, for example by twisting them together in line. I heat the joint with the iron and feed in enough solder to flow through all the strands, without making a blob. I let it cool without moving it, then check that it is smooth and that the insulation has not melted. Finally I slide the heat-shrink over the joint and shrink it with a heat gun so it covers all the bare metal.
markingPoints: Fits the heat-shrink sleeving onto the wire before soldering
Strips without cutting strands, then twists and tins
Makes a firm mechanical joint before soldering
Solder flows through the strands; joint not moved while cooling
Heat-shrink fully covers the joint, shrunk with a heat gun

essays.stem: Explain how heat can damage components and boards during soldering and de-soldering, and how to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Too much heat, or heat for too long, can damage parts such as transistors, diodes, LEDs and integrated circuits inside their bodies. It can also melt plastic parts and the insulation on wires. On the board, too much heat can make a copper pad or track lift off, which spoils the board. To prevent this, I use a temperature-controlled iron set as the maker advises, with a clean, tinned tip of the right size so that heat passes quickly into the joint. I keep the iron on each joint for only a few seconds. I clip a heat sink onto the lead of a sensitive part, between the joint and the body. I let a joint cool before I rework it. When de-soldering, I clear the solder with a pump or braid instead of heating and pulling, and I never force a part out.
markingPoints: Heat can damage sensitive parts, plastic and insulation
Heat can lift pads and tracks from the board
Uses a temperature-controlled iron with a clean, tinned tip of the right size
Keeps heating time short and uses a heat sink on sensitive parts
De-solders with pump or braid and never forces parts out

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect, clean and test a board after soldering, and how you would leave the work area.
essays.modelAnswer: I look at every joint with a magnifier. Each one should be smooth and shiny, with the pad covered and no bridges, cold joints or lifted pads. I check that every part is in the right place, the right way round and sitting flat, and I trim any long leads. If the flux is not a no-clean type, I clean the board with isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush and let it dry. Before any power is connected, I use a multimeter to check for a short across the supply connections. Then I test the circuit as the instructions say, using only the battery or low-voltage supply the assessor approves. Finally I switch off the iron, clean and tin the tip and put it in its stand, put solder scraps and clippings in the marked container, tidy my tools and wash my hands.
markingPoints: Inspects every joint with a magnifier for faults
Checks parts are correct, the right way round and flat
Cleans flux residue where needed
Checks for shorts with a meter before power; tests only with an approved low-voltage supply
Switches off and stores the iron, disposes of waste correctly, tidies and washes hands

practical1.title: Solder a set of components onto a practice board and build a battery-powered LED circuit
practical1.brief: Each member is given a practice circuit board (or stripboard), a layout drawing and a kit of through-hole parts: resistors, diodes, an LED, an electrolytic capacitor, wire links and a battery clip. Each member sets up a safe soldering bench, identifies each part and its value, fits it the right way round, solders every joint, trims the leads and inspects the joints with a magnifier. Members then check each other's boards for shorts with a multimeter. Only when the assessor has approved a board is it tested with a 9 V battery to light the LED. No mains-powered circuit is built or tested. Photograph each stage below for each member and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every board is finished and the benches are clean.
materials: Temperature-controlled soldering station with stand and damp sponge or brass wool (one per member)
Practice board or stripboard, layout drawing and a kit of through-hole parts (one per member)
Side cutters, long-nose pliers and a magnifier
Fume extractor, anti-static mat and wrist strap
Multimeter, and a 9 V battery with clip
photos: Each member's bench set up with stand, sponge, fume extractor and safety glasses
Parts laid out and identified against the parts list
Parts fitted on the board, the right way round, before soldering
The solder side after soldering, before trimming
A close-up of the finished joints after trimming
The LED lit from the 9 V battery after approval
The benches cleaned, with irons switched off and in their stands
checklist: Checked the iron, cable and plug, and set up the bench safely before starting
Identified each part and its value correctly, including the resistor colour code
Fitted the diode, LED and capacitor the right way round
Heated the pad and lead together and fed solder into the joint
Joints smooth and shiny with the pad covered, and no bridges, cold joints or lifted pads
Trimmed leads neatly while holding the ends, wearing safety glasses
Checked for shorts with a meter before the battery was connected
Left the bench clean, the iron off and in its stand, and washed hands
safety: Always return the iron to its stand; never touch the tip or the metal near it
Use the fume extractor and keep your face out of the fumes
Do not eat or drink at the bench; wash your hands after soldering
Wear safety glasses when soldering and trimming leads
Test only with the 9 V battery, and only after the assessor approves the board

practical2.title: De-solder and replace components, and make soldered wire joints
practical2.brief: Each member is given a scrap circuit board. Using a desoldering pump on some joints and desoldering braid on others, remove at least four components, including one part with three or more leads, without lifting pads or damaging tracks. Clean the holes, fit a new component in one of the places, and solder it. Next, each member makes two soldered wire joints: an in-line joint between two stranded wires, covered with heat-shrink sleeving, and a wire soldered to a terminal tag or solder cup. Members check each other's work with a magnifier and a multimeter on the continuity setting before the assessor inspects it. Photograph each stage below for each member and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Temperature-controlled soldering station with stand and damp sponge (one per member)
Scrap circuit boards with through-hole parts
Stranded hook-up wire, heat-shrink sleeving, and terminal tags or solder cups
Heat gun, side cutters, wire strippers and a magnifier
Multimeter, fume extractor and safety glasses
photos: The scrap board before any parts are removed
The desoldering pump being used on a joint
The braid being used on a joint
The board after parts are removed, showing clean holes and pads
The new part fitted and soldered
The in-line wire joint before and after the heat-shrink is shrunk
The wire soldered to the terminal tag or solder cup
The bench cleaned and the iron switched off in its stand
checklist: Set up and checked the soldering station and wore safety glasses
Used the desoldering pump correctly (set, heat, place, release)
Used the braid correctly, cutting off the used end each time
Removed parts without lifting pads or damaging tracks
Refitted and soldered a new part with a good joint
Fitted heat-shrink before soldering, tinned the wires and made a firm in-line joint
Soldered a wire to a tag or cup without melting the insulation
Checked continuity with a meter, left the bench clean and disposed of waste correctly
safety: Always return the iron to its stand; keep the cable away from the hot tip
Use the fume extractor and keep your face out of the fumes
Never pull or flick a part while the solder is molten; molten solder can spit
Do not eat or drink at the bench; wash your hands after work
Point the heat gun away from people, and do not touch the nozzle after use
